How are you hiding the transaction?
Using the filter. So View>Filter By, then uncheck "Reconciled". I usually do this because it's easier to see what the 'active' transactions are, so to speak.

That's what I thought you may be doing. With the recent changes, the auto-complete list of the description is recreated on every register update from the list of transactions so it can get the most recent order correct and also to reflect any changes to descriptions and possible deletions.

As you exclude the reconciled transactions, they will not be in the list to load in the register and hence those descriptions will not be in the list.

Not sure what can be done here but will have a think.

Does GnuCash not have all the transactions in memory somewhere? I.e., does it only load the ones that meet the filter condition? If so, I see the problem, but if they are all loaded, and only the filtered ones are displayed, then this seems solvable.

Yes all of the Gnucash data is held in memory. The problem is that the auto-complete description list is generated as part of the register view. The register is created from an incoming list of splits which has already been filtered to remove the reconciled ones and so the descriptions are not available.

Not able to match a reverse transaction of a previously matched transaction
Make sure the the online id is unset in the reverse transaction

As an example, consider an imported credit card purchase transaction for items you subsequently decide to return.  If you use reverse transaction to enter the reimbursement, the new transaction erroneously maintains the original online id which will prevent the new transaction from being available to be matched on a subsequent import.  To work-around the issue, you may use duplicate transaction to clear the online id.

The underlying cause of the problem is that Windows uses 16-bit characters for Unicode (UTF-16) and assumes that 8-bit characters are encoded in the locale's code page. Code pages are an archaic encoding scheme invented 40 years ago by IBM for the original DOS.

GnuCash uses an 8-bit multi-byte encoding called UTF-8; it's the standard encoding for Unix-based operating systems. That works fine except for path names on Windows that must be transcoded to utf-16. Windows takes the UTF-8 encoded file path and converts it to UTF-16 assuming that it's encoded in whatever your locale's code page is.

Bob's fix in https://github.com/Gnucash/gnucash/commit/fb58959f9a8a46e70e0486359b658d2e3084110e simply uses the Glib file-open function that knows to convert UTF-8 to UTF-16 on Windows. But the CSV exporter uses a C++ file stream to write the file and that has to be explicitly told (via imbue as Chris suggested in comment 5) to use UTF-8->UTF-16. That would work if we built GnuCash with Microsoft's compiler, but GnuCash isn't written in a way that that would work, so we use gcc and gcc doesn't support C++ localization on Windows so we need a different approach.
